description_full: Gogo Inc., together with its subsidiaries, provides broadband connectivity services to the aviation industry in the United States and internationally. The company's product platform includes networks, antennas, and airborne equipment and software. The company offers in-flight systems; in-flight services; aviation partner support; and engineering, design, and development services, as well as production operations functions. It offers voice and data, in-flight entertainment, and other services. In addition, the company's infrastructure includes networks, towers, cyber security software and data centers to support in-flight connectivity services, as well as in the provision of telecommunications services. The company sells its products primarily to aircraft operators and original equipment manufacturers of business aviation aircraft through a distribution network of independent dealers. Gogo Inc. was founded in 1991 and is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado.

financial_summary: Gogo Inc. is a small-cap communication services business with a $526M market cap on $910M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +31% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +2.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 8% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $65M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.63× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 25% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
